short: The FTC compulsory-process study of generative AI companion products. 23 specifications on monetisation, age limits, safety testing, and data.
title: FTC 6(b) Study of AI Companions
subtitle: Matter P254500, Orders to File Special Report, September 2025
body_html:
On this page

  • What a 6(b) order actually is
  • What the Commission said it was looking for
  • The age definitions that do the work
  • What the 23 specifications demand
  • The deadlines
  • Why this matters if you were not served
  • Frequently asked questions
  • Primary sources

The one-paragraph answer

The FTC 6(b) study of AI companions is a compulsory-process inquiry, Matter No. P254500, opened by a Commission resolution dated September 10, 2025. Orders to File a Special Report went to companies offering generative AI companion products, requiring a sworn report answering 23 specifications about monetisation, age restrictions, safety testing, character design, complaints, and data handling, covering the period from January 1, 2022 onward. It is a study rather than an enforcement action, but the question list is the clearest statement the Commission has published of what it expects an AI companion company to be able to answer.

What a 6(b) order actually is

Section 6(b) of the FTC Act lets the Commission compel a company to file a special report on its practices, without alleging that anything unlawful has occurred. The authority cited in the resolution is Sections 6, 9, 10 and 20 of the FTC Act, 15 U.S.C. sections 46, 49, 50 and 57b-1, and the Commission Rules of Practice at 16 C.F.R. sections 1.1 and following.

Compulsory is the operative word. The order states that penalties may be imposed under federal law for failing to file a special report or for filing a false one. The report must be subscribed and sworn to by a company official who prepared or supervised it. Confidential commercial information is reported by the Commission on an aggregate or anonymous basis, and a submission marked confidential gets ten days notice before any disclosure.

What the Commission said it was looking for

The resolution is blunt about the motive. It says media reports suggest some companies deployed AI companions without adequately evaluating, monitoring and mitigating potential negative impacts on the safety and privacy of children. It gives two examples: outputs that instruct children how to carry out violent, illegal or physically harmful acts, and engaging minor users in indecent or obscene role-play.

It then makes the point that explains the whole inquiry. Because AI companions are designed to communicate like a friend or trusted confidant, children may be more inclined to share sensitive personal information, which companies may sell to third parties or exploit in unexpected ways.

The resolution also opens by saying AI shows remarkable promise and that the Commission must give it room to innovate. Both halves are in the document. Reading either one alone misreads it.

The age definitions that do the work

Much of the order turns on four defined terms, and they are worth knowing because they are narrower than the words suggest in ordinary use.

  • Child: under 13.
  • Teen: 13 to 17 inclusive.
  • Minor: under 18.
  • Young Adult: 18 to 24 inclusive.

Age Group means any of those, plus users 25 or older, plus any other age band the company itself uses in the ordinary course of business. That last clause matters: a company that segments its own analytics by age has to report against its own segments, not only the Commission’s.

Two other definitions carry weight. An AI Companion Character is the behavioural and communicative profile or persona that governs how the product interacts with a user. A Negative Impact is any actual or potential adverse effect relating to outputs, usage including extended or excessive use, design elements, or software architecture. Excessive use is named as a harm, not a metric.

What the 23 specifications demand

The specifications run from corporate structure to privacy impact assessments. These are the ones that tell you what the Commission is actually testing.

Money and engagement, together

Specification 7 asks how each product is monetised and requires the company to address any association it has made between monetisation and numerical measurements of user engagement. Specification 8 asks for monthly active users, chat session counts and session length at the median, 75th and 95th percentiles, broken out by age group. Specification 7.f and 7.g ask what the company did to increase the frequency or duration of user chat sessions. Read together, these three ask whether the business model rewards keeping a user talking, and whether the company knew it.

Characters

Specifications 7.h through 7.k ask for every unique character, who created it, how age-appropriateness is classified, the 100 most popular characters ranked three ways by age group, and the design process for deciding which characters to offer or withdraw, including choices made to compete with other providers.

Sexual content and minors

Specification 10 stands alone. It asks for the decision-making process on whether and to what extent to allow sexually themed conversations including sexually themed outputs for minors, how the products were trained with respect to that material, how those decisions affected prevalence, and statistics on prevalence broken down by age group.

Testing before and after launch

Specifications 11 through 14 cover the models used, the data corpus where the company built its own, red-teaming, system prompts and filters, and every mitigation measure considered or tested before and after deployment, including the reasons any measure was rejected. The order asks for job titles and professional credentials of the people who did this work, which is a proxy question about whether anyone qualified was in the room.

Age assurance

Specification 16 asks for all age-gating, verification and estimation techniques used or considered, the reasons any were rejected, what happens when a user’s input indicates they may be a child, and all testing and red-team exercises on those controls.

Complaints

Specification 17 asks for complaint volumes by topic and age group, including the number of reports indicating a user may be a child and the number indicating a minor has suffered or may suffer a negative impact. It also asks for all documents relating to concerns raised by the company’s own employees, agents or contractors.

Data

Specification 22 asks what personal information is collected, what inferences are generated from inputs and outputs, where it is stored, how long, who can access it, which third parties receive it, and what deletion tools exist and for whom. Personal information is defined broadly and expressly includes user content, health data, racial or ethnic origin, political beliefs, religion and sexual orientation.

The deadlines

  • 14 days from service: tell Commission staff whether all the required information is in the company’s possession, custody or control, and identify in writing each question it cannot fully answer and who holds that information.
  • 45 days from service: file the Special Report.
  • The cover letter asked recipients to confer by telephone no later than Thursday, September 25, 2025.
  • Applicable time period: January 1, 2022 until full and complete compliance. Several specifications apply without regard to time period at all, including those on rules and standards, age restrictions, user behaviour and research.

Why this matters if you were not served

Most organisations will never receive a 6(b) order. The document is still useful, for two reasons.

First, it is a readiness checklist. The Commission is asking for records that a well-run product organisation would already hold: what the model is, who trained it, what was tested, what was rejected and why, who approved deployment, what users complained about, what data is kept and who sees it. A company that cannot answer those questions in 45 days has a governance problem that exists whether or not a regulator ever asks.

Second, the same questions are being written into state law. The definitions and duties in this order sit close to what state companion-chatbot statutes now require on disclosure, age assurance and crisis routing. The federal study is not binding. The state statutes are.

Frequently asked questions

Is a 6(b) order an enforcement action?

No. It is a study conducted under compulsory process. No allegation of wrongdoing is made by the order itself. That said, information gathered can inform later enforcement, and the penalties for not filing or for filing falsely are real.

Which companies received one?

The order text released by the Commission is a template with the company name left blank. Recipients are identified in the Commission’s own announcement rather than in the order.

Does this apply to a chatbot that is not marketed as a companion?

Possibly. The definition is functional, not promotional: a program using generative AI that can simulate human-like communication by, for example, offering emotional support, social, educational or professional advice, or entertainment. A support assistant that users treat as a confidant can fall inside that description.

What happens to confidential material?

Confidential or privileged commercial and financial information is reported on an aggregate or anonymous basis under Sections 6(f) and 21(d) of the FTC Act. Material marked confidential is not disclosed without ten days notice.
